source.title: High-Frequency Component Helps Explain the Generalization of Convolutional Neural Networks
source.authors: Haohan Wang; Xindi Wu; Ze-Yi Huang; E. Xing

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper through its references; no cutoff or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how frequency components and training choices relate to CNN generalization, using frequency-filtered inputs and accuracy-gap comparisons rather than the original interventions in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on natural-label and shuffled-label training, but the shuffled-label training curves are explicitly from training samples and do not report held-out accuracy for shuffled labels. That does not test V1's stated held-out comparison. The paper tests batch-size effects on training/test accuracy and compares dropout with the vanilla setup. Architecture and optimizer findings concern CNN frequency sensitivity and accuracy gaps, but do not compare convolutional with fully connected networks or adaptive-optimizer versus SGD held-out performance as V3 and V4 specify.
record.test_reason: The batch-size and dropout experiments directly compare held-out accuracy after changing the relevant training choice. These use the same intervention and outcome as V5 and V6; the additional frequency analyses do not make these comparisons a different method.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors propose frequency content as an explanation for several CNN behaviors: models exploit signals outside human visual preferences, some training heuristics encourage high-frequency reliance, and adversarially robust models tend to have smoother kernels. They present these as explanations and hypotheses, not proof that high-frequency reliance universally determines generalization.
record.recipe_differences: Frequency decomposition and evaluation of LFC/HFC responses; ResNet-18 CIFAR-10 vanilla setup uses Adam, learning rate 10^-4, batch size 100, Xavier initialization, and 100 epochs. This is not the original random-label generalization experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size changes the reported training/test accuracy and generalization-gap behavior. The paper also reports differences by architecture, optimizer, training heuristic, frequency radius, and whether training data are natural-label or shuffled-label.

fits_no_version.finding: Training on low-frequency components yields higher original-test accuracy than training on high-frequency components at all four radii.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Frequency content retained during training affects transfer to original CIFAR-10 test images.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger batches reportedly produce smaller training–test accuracy gaps despite lower testing accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A smaller generalization gap can accompany worse held-out accuracy when batch size changes.

record.problems: Batch-size and heuristic results are mainly presented as plots without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The stated batch-size comparison is limited to the paper's CIFAR-10 setup; other datasets are mentioned as appendix experiments without their results in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for training accuracies of the LFC/HFC-trained models; the Table 1 values relevant to generalization are the original-test accuracies recorded in R1–R8. Natural-label and shuffled-label training curves in Figure 3 are training-sample measurements and do not report the held-out random-label outcome needed for V1.

untested.parts: Figure 3 demonstrates comparable natural-label and shuffled-label training accuracy with different training durations, but provides no shuffled-label held-out accuracy. The full same-recipe memorization/generalization comparison is not established.
No width sweep or comparison beyond the width required for zero training error.
The architecture comparison includes only convolutional networks; no fully connected comparator or local-connectivity intervention.
The optimizer comparison reports frequency sensitivity, without adaptive-versus-SGD held-out performance or the specified tuning comparison.
No language-model experiment, identification of a batch-size threshold, or comparison of longer training, learning-rate scaling, warmup, or normalization and regularization adaptations.
No small-training-set comparison, dropout-strength sweep, or joint removal of dropout and weight decay with data augmentation.
No magnitude-aware weight-perturbation measure or ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. Spatial kernel smoothness is a different construct.
No removal and retraining comparison using memorized versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text preserves figure labels but not readable curve values. Batch-size and dropout judgments therefore rest on the authors' explicit qualitative descriptions. The study is not an original source for V5 or V6.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out accuracy is reported for the shuffled-label model, and the reported tests do not establish the claimed same-recipe natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold comparison.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks or test of local connectivity.
Optimizer comparisons do not report adaptive-versus-SGD held-out performance under the version's tuning conditions.
The batch-size plots do not establish a workload-dependent threshold or compare language models; the paper does not test the cited recipe adaptations.
The study tests dropout in its ResNet-18 CIFAR-10 setup, but not small training sets, excessive dropout, or joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison of generalization measures.
No removal of memorized training examples.
